stem: If v(t)=3t² in SI units, the acceleration at t=2 s is

choices.rationale: Reads the coefficient 3 in v(t)=3t² as the acceleration itself, as if v were proportional to t, instead of differentiating v(t) with respect to time.

Mistakenly differentiates v(t)=3t² using an incomplete power rule (dropping the exponent multiplier), computing dv/dt=3t instead of the correct 6t, then evaluates 3(2)=6 m/s² at the correct time t=2 s.
dv/dt=6t, evaluated at t=2 s gives 12 m/s².
Multiplies 6t by t again instead of substituting t=2, giving 6t²=6(2)²=24.

stem: The displacement from t=0 to T for v(t)=kt is

choices.rationale: Gives the final velocity v(T)=kT, which has units of speed rather than displacement; displacement requires integrating the linearly increasing velocity over the interval.
Integrates kt dt to kT² but drops the 1/2 factor that comes from the power rule.
integrating kt gives kT²/2
Divides the constant k by T, a quantity with units of acceleration per unit time, instead of integrating the velocity over the interval; it is not a displacement.

stem: A force F(x)=ax acts in one dimension. The work from 0 to L is

choices.rationale: Mistakes the endpoint force value F(L)=aL for the work itself, without multiplying by the displacement.
Multiplies the endpoint force F(L)=aL by the full distance L as if the force were constant, missing the 1/2 factor from integrating the linearly increasing force.
the integral of ax dx is aL²/2
Divides the force gradient a by L instead of integrating the force over the displacement; integrating ax always produces a term proportional to L², never a/L.

stem: A particle moves in one dimension under a conservative force with potential energy U(x). The force on the particle is given by which of the following?

choices.rationale: Drops the negative sign, forgetting that force opposes (rather than follows) the direction of increasing potential energy.
force is the negative potential gradient
Divides U by x instead of differentiating; -U/x equals -dU/dx only when U is directly proportional to x, so it is wrong for a general potential energy function.

This differentiates U twice. The second derivative is the curvature (stiffness) of the potential well and equals minus the rate of change of the force with position; it is not the force itself, which is −dU/dx.

stem: A power law P(t)=ct² delivers energy from 0 to T equal to

choices.rationale: Evaluates the power at time T and treats that instantaneous value as the total energy, without integrating over the interval.
Integrates ct² correctly in form but uses the wrong power-rule denominator, writing t³/2 instead of t³/3.
energy is the time integral of power
Differentiates P(t)=ct² instead of integrating it, computing d/dt(ct²)=2ct and evaluating at T.

stem: At a stable equilibrium x₀, U(x) has

choices.rationale: small displacements raise potential energy
Confuses stable equilibrium with unstable equilibrium, where the potential sits at a local maximum instead.
Assumes equilibrium requires the slope to blow up rather than vanish, misreading dU/dx=0 as an undefined or infinite condition.
Assumes equilibrium points must be non-smooth kinks in U(x) rather than smooth minima where dU/dx=0.
differentiate position with respect to time
Drops the coefficient 3 that the power rule brings down from At³, reducing the exponent without multiplying by it.
Reduces the exponent on At³ by one too many, an off-by-one power-rule slip giving t instead of t².
Gives only the cubic term At³ and drops the −Bt term; no derivative has been taken, so this is not a velocity expression at all.

stem: A force F(x)=F₀e^{-x/L} acts along the direction of displacement, with L a positive constant. The work done as the object moves from x=0 to x→∞ is

choices.rationale: Inverts the decay length, dividing by L instead of multiplying, as if the integral shrank rather than scaled by the decay length.
The integral ∫₀^∞ F₀e^{-x/L}dx = F₀L converges because L>0 makes the exponential decay (not grow) as x increases.
Assumes the force decaying to zero as x→∞ means the enclosed area (work) also vanishes, rather than converging to a finite nonzero value.
Assumes an infinite integration limit must always produce infinite work, missing that the exponential integrand decays fast enough to converge.
This is the first derivative, velocity, rather than acceleration.
Two time derivatives give v=4Ct³ and a=12Ct².
This differentiates a third time, one differentiation too many: d³x/dt³ = 24Ct.
This reduces the exponent without applying the power-rule coefficients.

stem: The signed area under a velocity-versus-time graph equals

choices.rationale: Acceleration is the slope of velocity versus time, not its area.
The time integral of velocity is the signed change in position.
Distance traveled adds all areas as positive, but signed velocity-time area gives displacement.
Change in velocity comes from integrating acceleration, not velocity.

stem: For U(x)=(1/2)kx² with k>0, x=0 is stable because

choices.rationale: The potential has positive curvature and a local minimum at equilibrium.
A local maximum corresponds to unstable equilibrium.
The force -kx varies with position and is not constant.
The chosen potential is nonnegative and energy sign is not the stability criterion.

stem: For m dv/dt=-bv, the characteristic decay time is

choices.rationale: This is the decay rate with units of inverse time, not the time constant.
The solution e^{-bt/m} has time constant τ=m/b.
This confuses the velocity-decay time with the faster decay time of kinetic energy.
This is the half-life, not the characteristic velocity-decay time m/b.

stem: A particle in uniform circular motion has

choices.rationale: This confuses constant speed with zero acceleration.
The velocity vector rotates continuously and is not constant.
Its changing velocity direction requires inward acceleration v²/r.
The net force is inward; an outward force is not required in an inertial frame.

stem: The work done from x=a to x=b by F(x) is

choices.rationale: Mechanical work along x is the position integral of force over the path.
This assumes the final force acts constantly over the entire displacement.
Averaging the endpoint forces is not valid for every F(x); it equals the integral only in special cases such as a force that is linear in position, so the word 'always' makes this false.
A time integral of force is impulse, not work.
This takes the derivative but omits the required negative sign.
The negative spatial derivative gives F=-dU/dx=-3Ax².
This keeps the negative sign but omits the power-rule factor three.
This divides by the exponent instead of multiplying by it when differentiating Ax³.

stem: At a one-dimensional classical turning point with total energy E,

choices.rationale: Potential zero depends on reference choice and is not the turning criterion.
At a turning point K=0, so total energy equals potential energy.
Force can be nonzero at a turning point and reverse the motion.
Kinetic energy is zero rather than maximum at the turning point.

stem: A force F acts on a particle with velocity v. Instantaneous power is

choices.rationale: Instantaneous mechanical power is the scalar product F·v.
A cross product gives a vector and does not represent energy-transfer rate.
This ignores the angle between force and velocity; only the parallel force component contributes to power.
Power is the rate of work, F·v; the product of force and acceleration F·a does not have units of power and is not the rate of energy transfer.
